caption:
The asteroid wiped out the dinosaurs 66 million years ago. So why did crocodiles make it through? A new study says their love of warm weather may be the answer.

Scientists led by University College London analyzed more than 7,000 fossils and records from over 400 living and extinct species. They combined that with computer models that rebuilt Earth's climate and geography across 245 million years. The study was published in Science Advances.

They found that crocodiles and their ancient relatives spent much of their 250-million-year history following warm climates rather than adapting to very different temperatures. When the planet got hotter, they expanded into new regions, sometimes as far as Antarctica. When it cooled, they moved back toward the tropics.

After the asteroid struck, the simulations suggest tropical and subtropical regions stayed suitable for crocodile relatives, even as habitats for many dinosaurs got much worse. Only the most extreme climate simulations wiped out those refuges.

Lead author Dr. Alfio Alessandro Chiarenza said crocodiles' long-standing preference for warm places "may have placed survivors exactly where suitable climates held up best, like around the equator." Those refuges could have sheltered populations that later recovered.

The team also points out that crocodile relatives were far more varied than today's species, from the giant "super croc" Sarcosuchus, up to 12 meters long, to small animals with faces like a pug.
